title: Balak: only the word I'm given (Numbers 22:38)
hook: Balaam can speak only the word God puts in his mouth
tomorrow: Balak: how goodly are thy tents

segments.voice: Yesterday, the donkey saw the angel three times before the famous seer saw anything. Your line was the donkey saw first. Whose quiet warning did you hear out? Day four hundred sixty-three.

You've been asked to give a toast, or write a reference, or say a few words at a meeting, and the person asking has made it very clear what they'd like you to say. Maybe they've even done you a favor. And the thing they want you to say isn't quite true. Balaam arrives in Moab in exactly that spot. King Balak meets him at the border, a little annoyed that he took so long, and promises him honor and reward. Everyone knows what the king is paying for. And Balaam's first words set the terms.
screen: `A TOAST, A REFERENCE, A FEW WORDS.` → `BALAK MEETS HIM AT THE BORDER.` → `BALAAM SETS THE TERMS.`

segments.voice: In the 1917 Jewish Publication Society translation, Balaam says: "the word that God putteth in my mouth, that shall I speak." He'd already told Balak's messengers something like it: even if the king gave me his house full of silver and gold, I couldn't go beyond the word of God. Then comes something close to comedy. Balak takes him up to a high place, builds seven altars, and offers sacrifices. Balak is waiting for a curse. Balaam opens his mouth, and out comes this: "How shall I curse, whom God hath not cursed?" Balak is beside himself. I brought you here to curse my enemies, he says, and you've blessed them. So he tries a different hilltop, the top of Pisgah. Seven more altars. Maybe from a new angle, the curse will come. It doesn't. Balaam says, in paraphrase, God has blessed, and I cannot turn it back. Then a third place, Peor. Same result. Three hilltops, twenty-one altars, and not one curse. A new view doesn't change what's true. The rabbis didn't treat Balaam as a hero for this. Rashi notices that, of all the things to mention, he brings up silver and gold, and reads it as a man who wanted the money and simply couldn't get around the word. That's what makes the scene interesting. Even someone who'd rather say something else can find that the true word is the only one that comes out. In the story, whatever was in his heart, his mouth was held to what God gave him, and the curse that was bought and paid for turned into a blessing.
screen: `ONLY THE WORD GOD PUTS IN MY MOUTH.` · `HOW SHALL I CURSE?` · `THREE HILLTOPS, TWENTY-ONE ALTARS.` · `A NEW VIEW DOESN'T CHANGE THE TRUTH.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: say only what's true today. Settle, and breathe. Think about the conversations ahead of you today. Is there one where you might be tempted to say what someone wants to hear rather than what's so? A compliment you don't mean, a promise you can't keep, a yes that's really a no. Find the true sentence you could say instead, kind and plain. Hold it in your mind. You don't need to be harsh; you only need to be true. Breathe with it until the bell. The bell holds the time.
Balak. The king who moved his hired seer from hilltop to hilltop, hoping for a curse, and got only the word God gave.
Your line: only the true word. Today, before you say something to please someone, check it once: is this actually true? Day four hundred sixty-three.

howItsDone: Balaam's oracles are read in the portion of Balak each summer, and Jewish commentators, starting with Rashi, read his words alongside the question of what was really in his heart.

original.note: Hebrew: the word that God puts in my mouth (Numbers 22:38).

trapdoor: what you thought: a prophet who refused a bribe.
what it means: a hired seer whose mouth could only give the true word, whatever he wanted.
what a scholar hears: Rashi on 22:18 reads 'silver and gold' as a sign of Balaam's greed; the three oracle sites (Bamoth-baal, Pisgah, Peor) each get seven altars.

notes: Numbers 22:38 and 23:8 quoted from JPS 1917; confirm wording.
Three sites: Bamoth-baal (22:41), the field of Zophim on the top of Pisgah (23:14), the top of Peor (23:28); seven altars at each, so twenty-one in all. Confirm count.
Rashi on 22:18: Balaam's mention of silver and gold shows he coveted others' wealth. Confirm.

Editor review (2026-10-01): removed 'opens his mouth to curse' (the text doesn't say he set out to curse at that moment; it says Balak wanted one) and framed the closing claim as 'in the story'. Quotes checked against JPS 1917.
